checks.claim: Key: the imaginary line through Earth's centre from the North Pole to the South Pole, which Earth spins around, is the axis
checks.note: Grokipedia: the axis is 'an imaginary line that passes through the geographic North and South Poles and the center of the planet'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The equator' is wrong: it runs around Earth's middle, halfway between the poles, not through the centre from pole to pole
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'an imaginary circumferential line', 'equidistant from the North and South Poles at 0 degrees latitude'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The orbit' is wrong: an orbit is a path around another body, not a line through Earth
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the gravitationally curved trajectory of an object'; Earth's orbit is its 365.25-day path around the Sun.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The horizon' is wrong: it is the apparent line between land/sea and sky
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the apparent line that separates Earth from the sky'.

checks.claim: Context: the axis's two ends are the North and South Poles; the equator runs around Earth's middle halfway between the poles; an orbit is the path Earth travels around the Sun
checks.note: All three statements match Grokipedia's Earth's rotation, Equator and Orbit pages.

checks.claim: Key: Earth spins once in about 24 hours
checks.note: NASA Space Place: 'a solar day is around 24 hours'; a sidereal day is 'almost exactly 23 hours and 56 minutes'. Either way 'about 24 hours' is true, and NASA's Earth facts page gives 'one rotation every 23.9 hours'. The 'about' makes the wording safe against the sidereal/solar distinction.

checks.claim: Second source on the two day lengths
checks.note: Grokipedia: sidereal day 23 h 56 min 4.09 s; mean solar day 'standardized at exactly 24 hours'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'About 12 hours' is wrong (only about half a turn)
checks.note: One rotation is 23.9 hours, so 12 hours is about half a turn, as the context says.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'About 30 days' is wrong (roughly a month)
checks.note: No defensible reading makes Earth's spin 30 days.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'About 365 days' is wrong; 365 days is a year, one trip around the Sun
checks.note: NASA: 'It takes 365.25 days to complete one trip around the Sun.'

checks.claim: Context: the spin is what a day is; 30 days is roughly a month; 365 days is a year, the time to travel around the Sun
checks.note: All true at grade level.

checks.claim: Key: day and night are caused by Earth spinning (rotation)
checks.note: Grokipedia: night occurs 'when a location on the planet's surface faces away from the Sun due to its axial rotation'; Earth's rotation page: 'This daily cycle produces alternating periods of daylight and darkness.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Earth circling the Sun' is wrong
checks.note: NSTA: 'Earth's revolution around the Sun is not why the Sun appears to move across the sky'; it 'is due to the spinning, or rotation, of Earth'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The Sun circling Earth' is wrong
checks.note: Grokipedia: the Sun's daily motion results 'from the Earth's rotation on its axis' and 'is entirely illusory'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The Moon blocking the Sun' is wrong (a known misconception; the Moon blocking the Sun is an eclipse, not night)
checks.note: Night is caused by facing away from the Sun, not by the Moon.

checks.claim: Context: the town is carried into the Sun's light (day) and round to the side facing away (night); Earth's trip round the Sun takes a year; the Sun does not travel around Earth
checks.note: True at grade level. The stem's town has daylight and darkness each day, so polar day/night does not arise.

checks.claim: Key: when it is noon at one place it is around midnight at the exact opposite side of Earth (the antipode)
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'Solar noon (i.e. the time at which the sun is highest) at one place is solar midnight at the other.' Grokipedia Antipodes agrees: 'inverted day-night cycles', 'a consistent 12-hour time difference'. Geometrically the Sun's altitude at the antipode is the negative of its altitude at the girl's spot, so if she has a bright Sun the boy is in darkness at every latitude and season. If 'noon' is read as clock noon, time zones and daylight saving can shift solar time by an hour or so, but 'Around midnight' still holds and is far the best choice.

checks.claim: Second source for noon/midnight at antipodes
checks.note: Grokipedia: when the Sun is at noon over one point it is 'at the nadir (midnight), over the other'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Around noon' is wrong
checks.note: The half facing the Sun has day and the other half night; the antipode is in the night half.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'Around sunrise' and 'Around sunset' are wrong
checks.note: Sunrise and sunset at the antipode fall about 6 hours either side of its midnight, i.e. when the girl's own place is at sunset or sunrise, not at her noon.

checks.claim: Context: only the half of Earth facing the Sun has day; the boy's side faces away, so he is in the middle of his night; his noon comes about 12 hours later
checks.note: Grokipedia Night: the half turned toward the Sun has daytime, the half turned away is dark; 12-hour offset per Grokipedia Antipodes.

checks.claim: Key: the Sun seems to travel across the sky from east to west
checks.note: Grokipedia: objects 'rise in the eastern horizon, traverse the sky, and set in the western horizon each day', an east-to-west progression 'for all observers on Earth'. True in both hemispheres: the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west in the Southern Hemisphere too, crossing the northern sky instead of the southern (Grokipedia Sunrise: due east at the equinoxes 'for observers in both hemispheres').

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'From west to east' is wrong (that is Earth's spin direction, not the Sun's apparent path)
checks.note: Grokipedia: Earth rotates 'from west to east', making the Sun 'appear to rise in the east and set in the west'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'From north to south' and 'From south to north' are wrong
checks.note: The rising point shifts north or south of east with the seasons, but the daily path runs east to west, never north-south.

checks.claim: Context: the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west; it only seems to move because Earth spins toward the east; the car-window analogy
checks.note: Grokipedia: sunrise 'typically in the east', caused by 'the planet's rotation on its axis from west to east'; Diurnal motion: 'entirely illusory'. 'Rises in the east' is true in the plain sense (due east only at the equinoxes). The analogy is apt: relative motion opposite to the observer's own.

checks.claim: Key: a girl whose shadow stretches out in front of her is facing away from the Sun
checks.note: The Schools Observatory (Liverpool John Moores University): 'The shadow always points away from the Sun.' Varsity Tutors 5th-grade lesson: 'a shadow forms on the side opposite the Sun.' Shadow in front means the Sun is behind her.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Toward the Sun' is wrong (the shadow would then be behind her)
checks.note: Shadow falls on the side opposite the Sun.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'With the Sun on her left' / 'on her right' are wrong (the shadow would fall to her right / left)
checks.note: Same rule; a side-lit person's shadow falls to the side, not in front.

checks.claim: Context: a shadow forms where an object blocks the light, so it always falls on the side away from the Sun
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'A shadow is a dark area on a surface where light from a light source is blocked by an object.'

checks.claim: Key: a stick whose shadow points west early in the morning has a shadow pointing toward the east late in the afternoon
checks.note: Varsity Tutors 5th-grade lesson: 'shadow direction shifts from roughly west in the morning to roughly east in the afternoon'. Grokipedia Sundial: the shadow moves 'from west to east' across the day.

checks.claim: Is it true everywhere, with no place fixed in the stem? (Southern Hemisphere, equator)
checks.note: Yes. The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west in both hemispheres (Grokipedia Diurnal motion, 'for all observers on Earth'), and a shadow always points away from the Sun (Schools Observatory), so morning shadows point roughly west and late-afternoon ones roughly east everywhere off the poles. Montana State's Southern Hemisphere lesson: 'If it is morning, the dowel's shadow should be pointing west.' What differs by hemisphere is the MIDDAY shadow (north in the north, south in the south; Schools Observatory) and the way it swings round (clockwise vs counterclockwise; Grokipedia Sundial). The question asks only about late afternoon, so no place is needed. In summer at mid-latitudes a late-afternoon shadow points east-southeast (NH) or east-northeast (SH), still nearest 'east' of the four choices.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Toward the west' is wrong (that is the morning direction)
checks.note: Late afternoon the Sun is in the west, and the shadow points away from it.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'Toward the north' / 'Toward the south' are wrong
checks.note: North or south is the MIDDAY shadow direction (by hemisphere), not the late-afternoon one; the 'roughly east' of the key covers the seasonal tilt toward SE/NE.

checks.claim: Context: in the morning the Sun is in the eastern sky so shadows point roughly west; by late afternoon the Sun is in the western sky so the shadow has swung round to point roughly east
checks.note: True in both hemispheres; 'swung round' does not commit to clockwise, so it is safe in the Southern Hemisphere.

checks.claim: Key: through a sunny day a flagpole's shadow is long, then short, then long again
checks.note: Science Friday: a shadow may 'start off in the morning long, get shortest some time around lunchtime' and is longest 'right before the sun goes down'. Grokipedia Sundial: 'shortest at solar noon'. True in the tropics too (where the noon shadow can vanish).

checks.claim: Shortest near midday = solar noon, not 12:00 on the clock
checks.note: Grokipedia: solar noon is when 'the Sun reaches its highest elevation' and 'occurs at the moment when the shadow is shortest'; it 'deviates' from clock noon. The question and context say 'around midday', which is safe; neither says 12:00.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Short, then long, then short again' is wrong (the reverse)
checks.note: Wikipedia: near sunrise and sunset 'shadows can be extremely long'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The same length all day long' is wrong
checks.note: Length follows the Sun's height, which changes through the day. (At the poles in polar day the Sun's height barely changes, but the stem has a sunrise and a sunset, so that case is excluded.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Long at first, then shorter all day' is wrong
checks.note: The shadow lengthens again after midday.

checks.claim: Context: longest early morning and late afternoon when the Sun is low; shortest around midday when it is highest; far from the equator the noon shadow never vanishes because the Sun is never straight overhead there
checks.note: Grokipedia: the tropics are 'the latitudinal limits ... where the Sun can appear directly overhead at noon'; NSTA: 'Do not teach that the Sun is directly overhead at noon' (never overhead from the continental US). 'Far from the equator' = outside the tropics (beyond about 23.4 degrees), true.

checks.claim: Key: a tree shadow many times longer than the tree is tall means the Sun is low in the sky
checks.note: Wikipedia: shadow length is 'proportional to the cotangent of the sun's elevation angle'. A shadow 3 times the height needs the Sun below about 18 degrees; 5 times, about 11 degrees: low. UCAR: 'When the Sun is low in the sky, a student's shadow will look longer.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'High in the sky' is wrong
checks.note: UCAR: 'When the Sun is higher in the sky, a student's shadow will be shorter.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Halfway up the sky' is wrong
checks.note: Halfway up (45 degrees) gives cot 45 = 1: the shadow is as long as the tree is tall, not many times longer.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Straight overhead' is wrong
checks.note: Grokipedia: with the Sun directly overhead, vertical objects 'cast no shadows'; nothing would stretch across the field.

checks.claim: Context: the lower the Sun, the more slanted its light and the longer the shadows; shadows longest near sunrise and sunset; a high Sun makes short shadows
checks.note: Matches UCAR and Wikipedia Shadow.

checks.claim: Context: 'a Sun straight overhead would leave almost none' (no shadows)
checks.note: True for an upright pole or person (Grokipedia Lahaina Noon: vertical objects 'cast no shadows'; UCAR 'little or no shadows'), but this question is about a TREE, and a tree's crown still throws a pool of shade right underneath it when the Sun is overhead (Wikipedia Shadow: with the Sun overhead 'shadows are cast directly underneath objects'). A child who knows trees give shade at noon could read this as false. Minor; key and choices are fine. Fix: '... and a Sun straight overhead would put the shadow right underneath, stretching no way at all.'

unit_notes: Every key and every wrong choice checks out. The shadow-direction question is safe everywhere (morning west / late afternoon east holds in both hemispheres; only the midday direction and the swing differ by hemisphere, and the unit never asks those). Length questions say 'around midday', never 12:00, and never put the Sun overhead outside the tropics. 'About 24 hours' for one spin is safe for both the solar day (24 h) and the sidereal day (23 h 56 m); NASA's Earth facts gives 23.9 h. The noon/midnight antipode question holds at every latitude and season; time zones can shift clock time by an hour, which 'Around midnight' absorbs. One minor wording flag in 39cd8405e8's context (an overhead Sun still leaves a tree shade beneath it). No quotations, named people, dates or changing numbers in the unit.
